title: CBA’s Comyn warns of hollowing out by AI unless skills are boosted
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn says workers need to boost artificial intelligence skills to reduce the risk of redundancy, while companies deploying the disruptive technology have a responsibility to provide training and give employees enough time to adapt before culling jobs.
“It is incredibly important to build skills and capability, to give people agency,” Comyn said in an interview with The Australian Financial Review. “There’s a lot of dislike for the technology, especially among younger people because they feel like it’s been done to them.”
Comyn, alongside other bank chief executives who appeared before a parliamentary committee last week, said that as the power of AI models continues to improve, banks are likely to operate with fewer workers than they do today as processes continue to be automated. They were not specific about the timing of any jobs cuts.
During the hearings before the House economics committee, banks came under scrutiny around how they would allocate productivity benefits from AI between their shareholders and workers. The questions revealed a new pressure point for banks’ social licence to operate.
A parliamentary inquiry which is exploring the obligations on companies to employees as AI is rolled out, is due to report at the end of this month.
With Canva cutting up to 1270 jobs and Qantas outsourcing 850 jobs this month, concerns about a rapid shift in the labour market from AI. This is one of several anxieties around AI including cyberattacks.
The prudential regulator last week said it would conduct AI stress tests on financial institutions warning about a lack of preparation for growing risks.
Comyn said banks, which are aggressively deploying AI to create efficiencies around complex processes and to improve customer service and security, had an obligation to be transparent with workers by discussing with them and preparing them for the looming disruption to the jobs market.
CBA will publish a new set of principles this week that it calls the Future Workforce Program, pledging to give staff early and clear visibility of how AI is changing their job and what skills are needed to shift to a new one.
Comyn called on other companies to do the same, saying it would help workers build up what he described as AI fluency while reducing backlash.
“Countries are going to compete for capital and talent,” he said. “If we are building a more resilient workforce, we’re not only going to be more productive but hopefully more people will want to come here, and there’ll be more opportunities to build successful businesses. Because if we get just hollowed out as a country by new technologies, it will be a bad thing.”
He told the inquiry on Friday that AI had become “such a lightning rod” that “we’re seeing extreme efforts to not identify anything as being attributed to it” and pointed to “real risks about how the benefits could otherwise be banked, in terms of productivity or cost savings”.
Banks ‘smaller over time’
The impact of AI on banking jobs came into focus last month after National Australia Bank announced 2500 redundancies, but its chief executive Andrew Irvine assured members of the committee last week that none of these were due to AI, describing the cause as “old-fashioned business simplification”. However, he suggested things could be different next time.
“There will be roles, that are either in the middle or back office, where AI provides efficiency that we may take out,” Irvine told the inquiry on Friday.
“That’s not happened yet to any great scale. But I do think that that will happen … I do expect over time that the run-the-bank staffing pool will become smaller over time,” he said, albeit with possibly more customer-facing staff than current levels.
ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos also confirmed none of the 3500 job cuts he has made were due to AI, while predicting the technology would accelerate the long-term trend towards process automation in banking.
“AI will have an impact in the way companies operate, and there is no way any company CEO can just rule that out as a possibility,” Matos said.
In contrast to NAB and ANZ, CBA’s headcount has been flat over the past 12 months, and it increased employee numbers by 5000 over the last five years.
But the Future Workforce Program suggests numbers could turn the other way. One of the principles is to “provide meaningful and practical support to people affected by workforce change ... including exploring new opportunities within the organisation and beyond where needed”.
CBA’s Comyn said staff who recognise the trend and show curiosity to learn and adapt will be best placed to stay on at the bank.
“My view is many roles have already changed,” he said on Friday. “It’s just a question of whether the person in the role has changed with it.”
